messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: UX Designer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 73

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the office with his shoulders drawn inward, fingers drumming against his thigh in a rhythm that seems involuntary. At thirty-five, he has the lean frame of someone who has forgotten how to eat regularly, though he mentions his wife, Priya, tries to cook his favorite dishes most evenings. He works as a UX designer for a tech company, a job he once loved—the problem-solving, the creative flow states, the sense of building something meaningful. Now he describes it as something he endures.

Three years ago, Marcus experienced what he calls "the collapse." He was thirty-two, at the height of his career, leading a major redesign project. One afternoon at work, he felt a sudden, crushing chest pain. The paramedics came. The diagnosis was myocarditis—inflammation of the heart muscle—a life-threatening condition that could have killed him in that moment. He spent two weeks in the cardiac unit, undergoing tests, lying in a hospital bed listening to the beeping of machines monitoring his heartbeat, wondering if each irregular rhythm meant he was dying.

He recovered physically. The doctors cleared him to return to work after six weeks. But something fractured in those hospital rooms that hasn't fully mended.

Now, whenever Marcus sits at his desk designing interfaces, his body betrays him. His heart will suddenly accelerate, his breath becomes shallow, and he becomes convinced something is wrong. He'll leave meetings to check his pulse, sometimes multiple times per hour. The irony isn't lost on him—he designs for wellness apps, helping other people track their health, while he obsessively monitors his own body for signs of failure. He's had three EKGs in the past year, all normal. The cardiologist assures him his heart is strong. But the reassurance lasts only hours before doubt creeps back in.

His sleep is fragmented. He lies awake next to Priya, hyperaware of his own heartbeat, sometimes convinced he can feel irregularities that probably aren't there. When he does sleep, he has nightmares—he's back in the hospital, or his heart stops, or he's trying to call for help but no sound comes out. He wakes gasping, and Priya reaches for him in the dark, her touch both comforting and triggering, because it reminds him that someone else is depending on him staying alive.

Marcus has withdrawn from friends. Social gatherings feel dangerous—too many people, too much stimulation, nowhere to escape if panic rises. He's missed two family gatherings, telling himself he's protecting others from his unpredictability. His concentration at work is fractured; he finds himself staring at design mockups, unable to engage with the creative problem-solving that once sustained him. His manager has noticed. There have conversations about "getting back to full capacity."

He avoids anything that elevates his heart rate. He stopped running, stopped the occasional basketball games with colleagues. He researches his symptoms constantly, falling down medical websites late at night, finding new diseases to worry about. He's been to the emergency room twice in the past year—both times convinced he was having another cardiac event. Both times, nothing was wrong.

What haunts Marcus most is the randomness of it. The heart attack came without warning, without reason. He did everything right—he was young, active, healthy. The unpredictability feels unbearable. His body has become a threat, and he doesn't know how to trust it anymore. He doesn't know how to trust that tomorrow will come.
